definition: Trenchant means sharp and effective; cutting straight to the point.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word trenchant. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know trenchant should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Her trenchant coaching notes run three lines apiece: what failed, why it failed, and the drill that fixes it.
A pointed remark has found its target but pricks rather than cuts; it stops short of trenchant.
Savage goes further than pointed by a long way — the critique now means to maul, sacrificing the fairness and precision that make a trenchant judgment stick.

A cutting remark is sharp enough to wound, and wounding may be all it does — plenty of cutting comments are simply cruel. Trenchant adds the part that matters: the cut lands exactly on the flaw, cleanly and fairly, so the target has to take it seriously.

Piercing goes straight through defenses — a piercing question, a piercing stare — and it measures penetration, not judgment. A trenchant analysis does more than get through: it cuts to the point that matters and settles something. Piercing reaches the nerve; trenchant reaches the verdict.

Trenchant comes from cutting: analysis or expression sharp enough to slice straight through padding to the point that matters.
A trenchant remark is not merely harsh — plenty of harsh remarks miss — it is accurate, economical and impossible to wave away.
Trenchant is praise with an edge: the analysis cuts cleanly to what matters.
Cutting and piercing can be merely cruel; incisive — a close twin you met earlier in this course — shares the same knife-work; blunt speech is honest but artless.
Use trenchant for criticism you want taken seriously, not just felt.

For decades, the town's founding story starred a heroic ferry captain who supposedly saved the settlement single-handed in the flood of 1911.
Then a retired archivist published a trenchant six-page essay in the historical society's bulletin.
She did not mock the legend or its lovers.
She identified the one claim the whole story rested on -- that the captain piloted the rescue alone -- and matched it against the ferry's own logbook, which lists a crew of nine.
The essay was fair, even affectionate, and it left the question settled: the lone-captain legend has not appeared in an official brochure since.
'She did not wound us,' the society's president admitted.
'She just found the exact soft spot and pressed once.'
